content: Joanna Tempowski served as the project manager for the WHO until July 2020 but is no longer affiliated with the organization. Annette Prüss-Ustün contributed to the WHO from 2011 to 2013. Marie-Noël Bruné Drisse worked in the Department of Food Safety, while Angelika Tritscher was part of the same department from 2011 to 2018 but is no longer with the WHO. In the Regional Office for the Americas, Agnes Soares da Silva and Ana Boischio were associated with the Department of Sustainable Development and Healthy Environment. In the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office, Mohamed Elmi worked at the Regional Centre for Environmental Health Action from 2011 to 2018 but is no longer with the WHO. Lesley Onyon, from the South-East Asia Regional Office, transitioned from the Department of Sustainable Development and Healthy Environment (until 2020) to the Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Health at WHO Headquarters. In the Western Pacific Regional Office, Rokho Kim moved from the Department of Health and the Environment (until 2020) to the Department of Quality Assurance of Norms and Standards at WHO Headquarters. In Ukraine, Dorit Nitzan, previously with the WHO Country Office, now works in the Health Emergencies Programme at the WHO Regional Office for Europe. Gerry McWeeney, who served from 2011 to 2018, is now with the WHO Office for Representation at the European Union. Professor Angela Mathee, Director of the Environment and Health Research Unit at the South African Medical Research Council in Johannesburg, specializes in public health, environmental epidemiology, and lead poisoning in African children. She declared no conflicts of interest. Professor Orish E. Orisakwe, from the Toxicology Unit at the University of Port Harcourt, Nigeria, is an expert in environmental and analytical toxicology and served on the roster of toxicological and epidemiological experts for the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) from 2011 to 2015. He also declared no conflicts of interest. Professor David Bellinger, affiliated with Harvard Medical School and Boston Children’s Hospital, chaired the guideline development group. His expertise includes the neurotoxic effects of lead, epidemiology, and environmental health. He has acted as an expert witness in litigation cases concerning neurodevelopmental harm caused by lead exposure, including work for the Kennedy-Krieger Institute in Baltimore. No conflicts of interest were identified in relation to the guideline development. Dr. Mary Jean Brown, formerly with the Lead Poisoning Prevention Branch at the CDC and now an adjunct assistant professor at the Harvard Chan School of Public Health, has expertise in the effects of lead on children’s health and the prevention and management of lead exposure. She was involved in the development of the LeadCare II point-of-care analyser for blood lead concentrations. No conflicts of interest were identified. Dr. Chulathida Chomchai, an associate professor of paediatrics and consultant at the Siriraj Poison Centre, Mahidol University, Thailand, specializes in paediatric toxicology, public health, and risk factors for lead exposure. She declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Aruna Dewan, from the Center for Education, Awareness, and Research on Chemicals and Health in Ahmedabad, India, focuses on clinical toxicology, analytical toxicology, and lead poisoning from traditional remedies. She also declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Thuppil Venkatesh, from the National Referral Centre for Lead Poisoning in India, specializes in lead screening, prevention of lead exposure, and analytical toxicology. He declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Yona Amitai, from Bar Ilan University in Israel, is an expert in paediatric toxicology, injury and poison prevention, and children’s environmental health. No conflicts of interest were identified. Professor Paul Dargan, a consultant physician and professor of clinical toxicology at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust in London, provided expert advice in support of legal action for compensation related to lead exposure in Kabwe, Zambia. No conflicts of interest were identified. Dr. Natalie Thurtle, previously a health advisor for Médecins Sans Frontières during the Zamfara heavy metal poisoning outbreak in Nigeria, now works at St George’s Hospital in Sydney, Australia. She specializes in clinical toxicology, medicine in low-resource settings, and the management of lead poisoning. She co-authored a paper on the outcomes of a humanitarian intervention providing chelation therapy to children in Zamfara. No conflicts of interest were identified.
